questions.q: What is a Service Level Indicator (SLI)?
options: A contractual promise made to a customer
A specific, measured metric that reflects user experience, such as percent of requests under 2 seconds
The amount of allowed downtime per month
A dashboard showing CPU and memory usage
questions.explain: An SLI is the actual measured metric, chosen to reflect what users experience — not everything you could measure, just the thing that matters.

questions.q: How does an SLA typically differ from an SLO?
options: An SLA is always stricter than the SLO
An SLA is the external, contractual promise, usually looser than the internal SLO, with penalties for missing it
An SLA and an SLO measure completely unrelated things
SLAs apply only to logs, not metrics
questions.explain: Teams deliberately set the SLO tighter than the SLA so they get an early warning and can react before ever breaching the real customer-facing contract.

questions.q: A service has an SLO of 99.5% success over 30 days. What is its error budget?
options: 99.5% of requests are allowed to fail
0.5% of requests are allowed to fail before the SLO is breached
There is no error budget unless there's an SLA
50% of requests are allowed to fail
questions.explain: The error budget is 100% minus the SLO — here, 100% - 99.5% = 0.5% of requests can fail before the objective is breached.

questions.q: Northbridge's checkout SLO is 99.9% over 30 days, giving roughly a 43-minute error budget. If an incident already burned 30 minutes of that budget, what should the team most likely do?
options: Immediately ship the riskiest planned release to make up for lost time
Ignore the budget since it's just an internal number
Be cautious about risky deploys until the budget resets, since only ~13 minutes remain
Declare a new SLA immediately
questions.explain: With most of the error budget already spent, the team has little room left before breaching the SLO, so the typical response is to slow down and avoid risky changes until the window resets.

questions.q: Why do teams use error budgets instead of just trying to prevent all failure?
options: Because zero failure is achievable and budgets are unnecessary
Because a numeric, pre-agreed budget turns 'can we ship this risky change' into a shared, objective decision instead of a subjective argument
Because error budgets eliminate the need for SLOs
Because customers prefer not knowing about failures
questions.explain: Error budgets give teams a shared number everyone already agreed to, replacing a subjective debate about risk with an objective check against remaining budget.
